memory_leads.memory: A large part of Greek-controlled deep-sea shipping is remembered as family-centered ownership groups using multiple vessel-owning companies while commercial decisions are coordinated through a family or group office, often associated with Piraeus and London. This private organizational layer can be economically important even when the operating fleet is globally deployed rather than domestic.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Family equity, relationship lending and willingness to buy or sell secondhand tonnage can make these groups active counter-cyclical asset traders, so ownership transfer may occur without a change in the physical fleet.
memory_leads.precision_note: The organizational pattern is recalled; group identities, ownership percentages and legal structures require later Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: Japan is remembered as having a deep layer of regional shipowners and tonnage providers, especially around Shikoku/Imabari-type maritime clusters, linked to local yards, banks and larger operators through long charters or management relationships. The vessel owner, shipbuilder, lender and commercial operator may be different entities.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: This network can preserve ordering and ownership capacity outside the balance sheets of the largest listed operators and can transmit local credit or yard conditions into global fleet supply.
memory_leads.precision_note: Regional concentration and contract conventions need primary-source verification.

memory_leads.memory: Beyond the largest global liner groups, an under-recalled layer of intra-Asia and regional container carriers includes names remembered such as Pacific International Lines, Regional Container Lines, Samudera Shipping Line, KMTC, Sinokor, SITC and Wan Hai in various periods. Their networks can be regionally dense even when they are small relative to global alliance carriers.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Regional carriers influence feeder competition, port-call density and the speed at which capacity is redeployed among Asian trades, so global alliance capacity alone can miss an important supply layer.
memory_leads.precision_note: Ownership status, network scope and historical ranking vary by period; the names are locator leads, not verified current classifications.

memory_leads.memory: Dedicated feeder operators remembered around X-Press Feeders and Unifeeder-type models provide common or relatively neutral feeder services connecting large transshipment hubs with smaller ports. They can carry boxes for multiple deep-sea lines rather than behaving as miniature global carriers.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Feeder availability and slot economics determine whether nominal mainline capacity can actually reach secondary ports; disruption or consolidation in this layer can change effective regional connectivity without changing deep-sea fleet size.
memory_leads.precision_note: Corporate ownership and neutrality practices changed over time and require Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: Mediterranean and European short-sea shipping includes family-controlled or regionally concentrated RoRo, RoPax and multipurpose networks remembered around Grimaldi-, Arkas- and Messina-type groups. These networks use different port pairs, cargo mixes and vessel economics from deep-sea container liner shipping.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Regional industrial demand, ferry/cargo mix and port access can move this fleet on a different cycle from global container shipping, while still competing with road, rail and feeder services for cargo.
memory_leads.precision_note: Company scope and family-control status must be checked at the relevant historical date.

memory_leads.memory: United States coastwise trades are remembered as a distinct cabotage ecosystem under Jones Act-type restrictions, with U.S.-flag/build/ownership/crewing requirements shaping domestic ocean services. Matson-, Crowley- and Pasha-type operators are remembered as examples in protected domestic trades including island or non-contiguous markets.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Entry barriers and replacement cost can make domestic vessel scarcity, yard capacity and regulatory waivers economically important in ways that are not visible in global freight indices.
memory_leads.precision_note: Exact statutory requirements, exemptions and route applicability require legal Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: Brazilian domestic shipping is remembered around the term 'navegação de cabotagem' and a policy/finance stack involving the Merchant Marine Fund (FMM) and an additional freight levy commonly remembered as AFRMM, alongside domestic shipping and shipbuilding support mechanisms.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: A dedicated domestic funding and levy system can alter the cost of fleet renewal, local-yard demand and the economics of substituting coastal shipping for road transport.
memory_leads.precision_note: Program design, rates, eligibility and chronology are not asserted and require Portuguese-language primary Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: Nigeria is remembered as having a cabotage/local-content regime administered through maritime authorities, with the Cabotage Vessel Financing Fund (CVFF) recurring as a policy instrument intended to support domestic vessel ownership or participation. Offshore-support and coastal trades are part of the remembered context.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Local-content rules and constrained vessel finance can change who captures offshore/coastal demand and whether domestic fleet capacity expands when commodity activity rises.
memory_leads.precision_note: Legal dates, disbursement history and institutional names must be verified; this is a source-discovery lead only.

memory_leads.memory: Indonesia is remembered as a particularly important domestic-shipping system because of archipelagic geography and cabotage policy. Pelni, Meratus-, Temas- and SPIL-type operators recur in memory, while 'pelayaran rakyat' refers to a traditional/small-vessel people's-shipping segment that is largely invisible in global liner atlases.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Domestic distribution can depend on small and regional vessels, so island connectivity, fuel, port access and local fleet renewal can matter independently of international container rates.
memory_leads.precision_note: Actor status and the formal definition of pelayaran rakyat require Indonesian-language Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: The Japanese term '内航海運' (naikō kaiun, domestic/coastal shipping) is remembered as covering a large ecosystem of smaller owners and operators moving industrial and energy cargo around Japan. '船主' (senshu, shipowner) and related local terminology can reveal entities that disappear when research searches only English names of the major shipping groups.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Domestic industrial production, refinery/power demand and local vessel renewal can create a coastal cycle partly distinct from international dry-bulk, tanker and liner markets.
memory_leads.precision_note: Translation and institutional segmentation should be checked against Japanese sources before factual use.

memory_leads.memory: Traditional dhow and small general-cargo networks are remembered as continuing to connect parts of the Gulf, Iran, Oman, western India and East Africa alongside containerized trade. These privately owned vessels and trading relationships can use secondary ports and cargo-handling practices poorly represented in global fleet datasets.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Sanctions, border rules, fuel costs and local trade demand may reroute or suppress this capacity without showing up cleanly in standard liner or bulk indices.
memory_leads.precision_note: Routes, vessel types and regulatory status vary widely; exact claims require regional Evidence.

memory_leads.memory: At draft-constrained or roadstead ports, local lighterage fleets and ship-to-ship transfer can form a distinct capacity layer between ocean vessels and shore. Chattogram/Chittagong-type outer-anchorage lighterage is one remembered example of a larger pattern in which many small operators mediate bulk or general cargo discharge.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: A shortage of lighters, pilots, tugs or safe transfer windows can create port congestion and demurrage even when berth or ocean-fleet capacity appears adequate.
memory_leads.precision_note: Named-port practices and operator structure require local-source verification.

memory_leads.memory: Indian cabotage restrictions and later relaxations are remembered as interacting with feeder economics and the use of foreign transshipment hubs such as Colombo. Policy treatment of coastal carriage can therefore influence whether Indian containers relay offshore or through domestic hubs.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: A regulatory change can alter sailing patterns, feeder demand and domestic hub utilization without any change in underlying import/export volume.
memory_leads.precision_note: The timing and cargo-specific scope of relaxations require authoritative Indian sources.

memory_leads.memory: The atlas names major global hubs, but a separate remembered topology uses Caribbean relay/transshipment nodes such as Kingston-, Freeport-, Caucedo- and Colón/Manzanillo-type hubs to connect mainline services with smaller island and regional ports.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Mainline network changes or terminal disruption at one relay hub can propagate into many small markets whose local demand would never justify direct deep-sea calls.
memory_leads.precision_note: Hub roles and relative importance change by carrier network and period.

memory_leads.memory: Useful source-discovery aliases for shipowner/shipping-company concepts include remembered terms such as French 'armateur', Spanish/Portuguese 'armador', Italian 'armatore', German 'Reederei', Dutch 'rederij', Scandinavian 'rederi', Spanish 'naviera' and Greek 'εφοπλιστής' for a shipowner. English-only search can systematically miss local corporate and trade records.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Recovering local owner names and predecessor entities is necessary to trace asset ownership, failures and restructurings across long cycles.
memory_leads.precision_note: Meanings and grammar vary by language; every term must be validated in the relevant source context.

memory_leads.memory: Remembered search vocabulary includes Portuguese 'cabotagem', Spanish 'cabotaje', Turkish 'kabotaj', Japanese '内航海運', Chinese '沿海运输' and '内贸' in domestic-trade contexts, and Indonesian 'pelayaran rakyat'. These terms can expose local regulations, trade associations and operators absent from English historical summaries.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Local terminology is often the bridge from a global cycle hypothesis to the actual domestic institutions that control market entry, vessel eligibility and port connectivity.
memory_leads.precision_note: This is a search-archaeology vocabulary list, not a claim that the terms are legally equivalent.

memory_leads.memory: Large transshipment hubs and port bottlenecks surfaced repeatedly while recalling regional networks, but the supplied atlas already treats ports, congestion and effective capacity as first-order mechanisms.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Retained only as a duplicate signal; P002 adds value mainly through feeder and secondary-port topology rather than repeating the generic port-bottleneck thesis.

memory_leads.memory: Global liner alliances, consolidation and mega-ship network effects reappeared as background to regional feedering, but these mechanisms are already explicit in the supplied atlas.
memory_leads.cycle_connection: Retained as a duplicate to distinguish regional-network novelty from already-covered global liner structure.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.assessment: The model recalls feeder dependence, local-content debates and many changing small operators, but not enough stable actor/alias detail to retain a specific lead without drifting into guesswork.
Regional shipping and ferry/bulk activity are remembered, but company lineage and local-language aliases are too uncertain for a bounded retained lead.
Cabotage and coastal services are remembered in several countries, but specific predecessor names and ownership histories are too unstable to record without Evidence.

The model recalls substantial inter-island/coastal activity and several possible carrier names, but confidence in historical ownership, aliases and continuity is insufficient to keep a specific lead in this pass.

novelty_summary.assessment: The regional/private lens produced high marginal novelty, especially in family ownership, domestic cabotage finance, independent feedering and local-language discovery vocabulary. Late recall increasingly became country-specific chronology or unstable actor names, so the pass stopped rather than expanding into an exhaustive national grid.

method_observation.observation: Local-language institutional terms and domestic-trade labels unlock materially different actor classes than an English/global-company atlas, but recall quality falls quickly once the prompt turns into a country-by-country name list. A sparse terminology lens is useful; exhaustive geographic enumeration is not.

stop_reason: The four preset questions were answered with specific retained leads and explicit no-specific-memory regions. Marginal recall then shifted toward uncertain company lineages, legal dates and country-by-country enumeration that require Evidence or would violate the sparse-map stop rule.
